item.title: Community Live Session: Specialized AI Agents for Smarter Customer Support Triage
item.dc:creator: Marina
item.description:
Community Live Session: Specialized AI Agents for Smarter Customer Support Triage
Public · Created by Marina
November 18, 2026 5:00 PM (Europe/Prague) → November 18, 2026 5:45 PM (Europe/Prague)
with-make.wistia.com/live/events/edlwk5dxgu?utm_campaign=Community&utm_source=Community&utm_medium=Community

What if one AI didn’t have to do everything?

On Thursday, November 19, @mszymkowiak will build a support triage workflow live, with Jev (TypeSafe’s new classification model) deciding where each ticket goes, specialized Make AI Agents preparing the case, and a human always making the final call.

How It Works

A customer writes in and a ticket appears in Freshdesk. Make picks it up instantly through a Freshdesk automation, with no polling.

Jev, TypeSafe’s new classification model, makes three quick decisions: which team should handle the ticket (Customer Support or Complaints), how frustrated the customer is, and whether it needs action today. Each answer comes with a confidence score.

A router raises the priority in Freshdesk if the ticket is urgent or the customer is frustrated. It then sends the ticket to the right specialist: a Customer Support agent or a Complaints agent. Each agent lives in its own subscenario with its own instructions.

The agent looks up the order in a Google Sheet that acts as the order database. It only uses what it finds there: if there’s no order number, it asks for one instead of guessing. It then writes an internal note (what the customer wants, the order status, what’s missing, and the suggested next step) plus a draft reply.

A human makes the call. The note lands on the ticket as a private note, with Jev’s decision and confidence at the top. Someone on the team reviews it, edits the draft, and replies. The AI never writes to the customer.

If Jev isn’t sure where a ticket belongs, or it isn’t a customer matter (an out-of-office reply, for example), no agent runs and the note simply asks a person to take over.

What You’ll Learn

What Jev is and why a classifier, not an LLM, is the right tool for routing decisions
How to use Jev’s confidence scores to decide when not to trust the AI
How to split one scenario into an entry point and a reusable main scenario (Call a scenario / Start scenario / Return output)
How to give a Make AI Agent a tool so it works with real data instead of guessing
Where to put the human in the loop

Not on Freshdesk?
No problem. Only the last modules touch the helpdesk. Everything after the input step reads from a set of variables, so to use HubSpot or any other system with a Make app or an API, you only swap the first modules and keep Jev, the router, and the agents as they are.

Who It’s For:

Support, operations, and automation builders who want faster ticket triage with AI, without giving up control over what customers actually receive. If you’ve ever wondered how much to trust an AI agent with customer-facing work, this one is for you.

Stick around for Q&A at the end — bring your questions, your own interview workflow, or just your curiosity.

item.title: I built an AI-assisted meeting follow-through system using Make, OpenAI and Google Workspace
item.dc:creator: Kanika
item.description:
I would like to look at something that is frequently ignored in the automation of meetings. It is useful to record what has been discussed, but how can we ensure that the decisions actually result in action?

I created a workflow that uses AI to link together the notes from meetings with action tracking, deadline monitoring, and change management.

How it works

  1. Meeting Notes Intake: Meeting notes are entered via a Google Form.

  2. AI-assisted extraction: OpenAI looks over the notes to detect the action items that have been suggested and arranges them in a uniform format.

  3. Human review: The proposed actions are placed in a Review Queue so that a person can check and approve them before they are included in the Action Register.

  4. Deadline monitoring: Keep an eye on the deadlines that are coming up and prepare draft emails to be sent via Gmail for review.

  5. Change Log: The updates relating to the tracked actions are kept so that any changes made to the original plan can be seen.

  6. Follow-up dashboard: This provides a central overview so that you can keep track of the actions still needed, the deadlines, and the progress.

One aspect that I especially wanted to look at was the Change Log.

The plans for a project rarely remain precisely the same as those agreed upon in the initial meeting, for priorities may change, deadlines may be altered, and the actions may be modified.

It is more difficult to tell whether the present action plan still agrees with the original decisions if there is no record of the changes.

The Change Log offers insight into the way the plan develops. It enables people to see what changes have been made and to decide whether the current commitments are still in line with the agreed direction. It does not automatically make that decision. The aim is to provide people with a clearer record based on which they can work.

A few design decisions behind the workflow:

The AI suggests courses of action, but a person has to approve them.

  • Emails sent as follow-ups are prepared in draft form and are not automatically sent.
  • Changes are kept on record rather than simply overwriting the original plan.
    The dashboard shows progress on various actions in one place.

I used Make, OpenAI, and Google Workspace, focusing on practical automation and human supervision rather than building another meeting summariser.

I’m attaching a brief walkthrough which shows how the workflow fits together.

I’d be interested to hear from other Makers:

What is your approach when it comes to altering action items or deadlines after a meeting? Do you keep a separate change history, or do you make the changes directly in the action tracker?

item.title: Zoho CRM V8: safe recovery after a write loses its response, without blind retry
item.dc:creator: Uwe_Krause
item.description:
What is your goal?

Recover safely when Zoho CRM V8 accepts a write but its response is lost, while preventing a second potentially non-idempotent action. Make orchestrates the workflow; ambiguous outcomes must remain locked for read-only reconciliation or manual review.

What is the problem & what have you tried?

Hello,

We have a stable command ID, an immutable payload hash, a persistent conditional claim before dispatch, and read-only recovery. When the remote outcome is unknown, the claim stays consumed and no automatic resend is allowed. Existing record IDs and source identities are kept separate from command IDs.

We reviewed these discussions:

Make Core — Automatic retries, Retry handler settings, and Airtable upsert safety Questions
What is your goal? Build a safety-critical Make Core workflow that prevents duplicate Airtable writes after errors or timeouts, requires human review before failed executions resume, and preserves reliable audit evidence. What is the problem & what have you tried? I’m preparing an inactive scenario for testing and need to verify several Make platform behaviors before activation. I’ve reviewed Make’s documentation on automatic retries, incomplete executions, and Retry erro…
How Can I Prevent Duplicate Records When a Make Scenario Runs Again? Beginner Questions
What is your goal? I want to build a Make scenario that processes incoming form submissions and stores the results in a spreadsheet or database without creating duplicate records. What is the problem? I’m trying to figure out the best way to check whether a record already exists before creating a new one. I know I could search for a matching email address or unique ID, but I’m unsure how to handle cases where multiple submissions arrive close together or the scenario runs …

The remaining case is: CRM accepts a write, the response is lost, and the orchestrator cannot establish completion. A search-before-create check or writing a processed flag after the CRM call leaves this gap. Upsert can prevent another entity being created, but may still execute updates or side effects again.

  • Has anyone implemented a documented Zoho V8 pattern that reconciles this case without repeating a potentially non-idempotent action?
  • Which Make retry paths must be accounted for, beyond the Retry handler setting, including connection errors and incomplete execution replay?
  • For simple field assignments with controlled side effects, what evidence supports using desired-state verification instead of an operation receipt?
  • Is there an established simpler pattern than a guarded single writer plus read-only reconciliation, while keeping ambiguous cases for manual review?

We are looking for tested examples or manufacturer documentation, not an exactly-once claim based solely on sequential processing. Please distinguish successful record deduplication from successful execution recovery. No production data or private configuration is included.

Thank you.

item.description:
I’m Vlad, founder of Usatii, a U.S.-based software engineering and AI integration company headquartered in Rochester, New York. We help organizations move beyond isolated automations toward complete, intelligent business systems.

Make.com is a great orchestration platform, but connecting applications is often only a part of the problem. A bigger challenge is to connect the underlying business processes, data, employees, decisions, and actions so work can be completed end-to-end reliably.

What we can help you accomplish

  • Advanced Make.com development: Multi-step scenarios, routers, iterators, aggregators, webhooks, HTTP requests, complex data mappings, custom API integrations, error handling, performance optimization, and troubleshooting existing implementations.

  • Enterprise AI integration: Integrating OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other models into operational workflows. This includes intelligent document processing, AI agents, business-data retrieval, structured decision-making, tool execution, and human approval mechanisms.

  • Custom software and integrations: Developing the missing infrastructure behind automations, i.e. REST APIs, databases, backend services, administrative dashboards, employee portals, native mobile applications, and integrations with business software.

  • Complete operational automation: Connecting sales, CRM, estimating, inventory, procurement, finance, scheduling, field operations, and customer communications into workflows that span multiple departments. We build systems with authentication, access controls, audit histories, exception handling, monitoring, and recovery mechanisms.

  • Agency and implementation partnerships: Working alongside Make specialists, consultants, and agencies that require additional software engineering capacity for complicated implementations.

Our experience

One of our most substantial implementations is an integrated operations platform for REBUILDIT INC., a construction company operating in Sacramento, California. We developed a shared operational system connecting customer intake, project management, estimating, scheduling, field employees, purchasing, inventory, financial context, and management reporting.

The important engineering decision was to model the relationships between customers, jobs, personnel, resources, and business actions. That system is an example of our broader software engineering capabilities.

We’ve also developed operational AI assistants, human approval queues for AI-generated actions, document generation, native iOS applications, business communications infrastructure, and permission-aware administrative systems.

How we approach AI and automation

We believe the next generation of enterprise automation will go substantially beyond predefined triggers and actions. An AI system should be able to understand the relevant business context, retrieve authorized information, evaluate what needs to happen, and execute appropriate actions across multiple systems.

We also recognize that not every problem needs an AI agent or custom-built application. If Make can accomplish the job efficiently, that’s what we should use. If an integration requires custom engineering, we can develop what is missing.

Our engagement model

We take a forward-deployed engineering approach: work directly with the people responsible for a process, identify the underlying bottleneck, establish measurable success criteria, and implement a working solution.

For appropriately scoped engagements, we offer selective free discovery and pilot development so organizations can evaluate a real use case before committing to a larger implementation.

We can also take on smaller, fixed-scope Make.com assignments or collaborate with agencies on larger software projects.

Our philosophy is that organizations should retain control over their operational data, proprietary software, and the intelligence generated by their systems. We structure ownership and licensing accordingly, while respecting the separate licensing requirements of platforms such as Make.

If you’re dealing with a difficult integration, an unreliable Make scenario, or a business process that needs more than standard automation modules, I’d be interested in understanding the problem. Reply here or send me a message explaining what applications are involved, what you’re trying to accomplish, and where your implementation falls short.

item.title: Automating Relationship Milestone Tracking with Date and Time Calculations
item.dc:creator: Scarlett_Lyng
item.description:
What is your goal?

My goal is to build an automated date-tracking workflow using Make.com that calculates elapsed time between a user-defined starting date and the current date.

For example, a user could enter a relationship anniversary, project launch date, or another important milestone. The automation should calculate the elapsed duration in days, hours, minutes, and seconds.

I’d like to explore how Make.com can handle date parsing, timestamp conversion, timezone management, and automated updates without requiring manual calculations.

What is the problem & what have you tried?

I’m exploring different approaches to implement this workflow efficiently.

One possible solution is to use Make.com’s date and time functions, variables, and mathematical operations to calculate the difference between two timestamps.

However, I’m trying to understand a few technical challenges:

How can I reliably convert user-provided dates into Unix timestamps?

What’s the best approach to handle different timezone settings?

How can I calculate elapsed days, hours, and minutes without incorrect rounding?

Can a scenario automatically update the calculated duration at scheduled intervals?

Would using a webhook with a frontend date calculator provide a more scalable architecture?

For reference, this is an example of the date-calculation concept I’m exploring: https://kalkulatorjadian.net/

I’d appreciate suggestions for building this workflow using native Make modules and functions rather than relying heavily on external services.

Error messages or input/output bundles

No specific error encountered yet. I’m currently researching the best implementation approach.

Example input:

{
“start_date”: “2026-01-15T10:30:00”,
“timezone”: “Asia/Jakarta”
}

Expected output:

{
“elapsed_days”: 288,
“elapsed_hours”: 6912,
“elapsed_minutes”: 414720,
“status”: “calculated”
}

The expected values are illustrative and will depend on the actual execution timestamp.

Create public scenario page

Kalkulator Jadian

Kalkulator Jadian — Hitung Hari Pacaran & Anniversary

Hitung hari jadian, lama pacaran dalam tahun, bulan, jam, menit, dan detik. Cek anniversary, milestone, dan unduh kartu kenangan. Gratis tanpa akun.

item.title: 🔥 Feature Spotlight: Maia Updates for Plan Mode, Memory, and Resolve Error
item.dc:creator: a_garcia
item.description:
Maia Updates Help You Plan, Build, and Fix Make Scenarios With More Context

Review the full approach before anything changes in your scenario, carry your preferences from one chat to the next, and go from a failed run to a fix you review before saving.

Maia updates are here, and they cover your work from planning through debugging.

What’s New in Maia Updates

  • New Plan mode: Plan asks all its questions up front, shows the modules, assumptions, and approach, and starts building only once you approve the plan. It also checks connections, app capabilities, and plan-tier access along the way, so problems show up before the build. Build stays the default: Maia asks questions one at a time and builds after you approve each step. Both modes work for new and existing scenarios.
  • Memory: Save private preferences about the apps and accounts you use or avoid, your preferred response detail, and language. Memory is saved per user, per team, and teammates never see yours. You can store up to 50 memories of 200 characters each, and you can add, edit, delete, clear, or turn off memories at any time.
  • Attach image: Upload, drag and drop, or paste up to three PNG, JPEG, or WebP images per session, up to 1.5 MB each. Maia reads each image once, and Make does not store it.
  • Resolve error: Maia reads your run data to see what passed through a module, where a run stopped, and whether the issue has happened before. Click Resolve error, and Maia revises the scenario from that data. You review the change before saving.
  • Copy response: Copy any Maia response in one click and paste it as markdown into Slack, documentation, or another chat

Maia Updates Use Cases for Make Automation

  • Review a proposed multi-step lead routing scenario in Plan mode before Maia adds modules to your scenario.

  • Save your preferred apps and response style, so you do not need to restate them in every new chat.

  • Drop in a sketch, whiteboard snapshot, or screenshot of a workflow, and ask Maia to build from it.

  • Open a failed run, ask Maia to find where the data stopped moving, and click Resolve error to review a revised scenario.

  • Copy Maia’s diagnosis of an error into Slack or shared documentation so teammates get the full breakdown without a rewrite.

Availability

Maia is available in open beta on all paid plans. On Free plans, Maia is available for a 30-day trial starting from signup.

Happy automating!

Andy the Maker

item.title: Lead Pipeline set up help please

item.description:
What is your goal?

To build a lead tracking pipeline for event ticket sales that retains 100% of customer identity and attribution data server-to-server.

The pipeline should flow from Meta Ads → WordPress/Elementor Landing Page (with Ticket Tailor checkout widget) → Make → HubSpot CRM.

When a sale happens, Make needs to check if the contact exists in HubSpot, update or create them, and create an associated Deal passing along the UTM traffic source metrics.

What is the problem & what have you tried?

The problem is that standard browser-based cookie tracking drops lead data during the user journey, resulting in data gaps inside HubSpot.

I know I need to bridge this server-side via Make to prevent data loss from tracking restrictions, but I do not have a technically capable way to integrate these platforms or structure the scenario data logic yet.

Specifically, I am unsure how to configure the embedded Ticket Tailor widget to capture the URL UTM parameters from the initial Meta ad click, pass them into the Ticket Tailor webhook payload, and how to structure the multi-object conditional routing (Search Contact → Router → Update/Create Contact + Create Deal) inside Make.

item.title: Hiring: connect multiple Gmail, Yahoo, Hotmail, Discord and personal WhatsApp accounts to Claude through the Make MCP server
item.dc:creator: Justadude
item.description:
Hi everyone,

I’m looking to hire a Make expert to build a cloud setup that connects all my messaging accounts to Claude through the Make MCP server. I want Claude to be my one place to read, reply to, and organize every inbox and chat.

The goal

Right now my messages are spread across many accounts. I want to open Claude, ask “what came in today?” and get one answer that covers everything. Then I want Claude to reply, sort, and clean up for me. Everything should run in Make’s cloud so it works even when my computer is off.

Accounts to connect

  1. Gmail: several accounts
  2. Yahoo Mail: two or three accounts
  3. Hotmail (Outlook.com): one account
  4. Discord: my personal DMs matter most. I don’t need server channels.
  5. WhatsApp (personal, not Business): I currently use TimelinesAI and want to replace it if there’s a good option.

What Claude should be able to do in every account

  1. Read new and older messages
  2. Search across all accounts at once
  3. Write and send replies and new messages
  4. Organize: labels, folders, archive, mark as read, delete junk
  5. Summarize: a daily rundown of what needs my attention

How I picture it working

  1. Each account gets connected to Make once.
  2. Make scenarios do the actual work (read, send, label, and so on).
  3. Those scenarios are exposed as tools through the Make MCP server.
  4. Claude connects to that MCP server and uses the tools when I ask.

If that’s the wrong way to think about it, tell me.

Please answer these in your reply

  1. Is this possible? Which parts work well and which don’t?
  2. Which Make app or module would you use for each account, and where would you need a workaround (for example IMAP for Yahoo)?
  3. Personal WhatsApp without TimelinesAI: what are my options, and how big is the risk of my number getting banned?
  4. Can Make read personal Discord DMs, or only bot and server messages? If not, what would you do instead?
  5. How would you keep this safe with full access? For example, an approval step before Claude sends anything.
  6. With this many accounts, roughly how many Make operations and which Make plan will I need each month?
  7. If there’s a better tool than Make for any part of this, say so. I’m open to it.

What I need from you

  1. An example of something similar you’ve built
  2. A fixed price for the build
  3. A monthly price for upkeep if something breaks
  4. How long it will take you

Handover

I’m not a developer. Please explain each piece in plain, simple steps, and include a short written guide or screen recording that shows how it works and how to fix common problems.

Budget and timeline

Open to quotes. Tell me your price and how long you need.

Reply here or send me a DM. Thanks!
